According to what you have chosen, the distinction between the Book and the Balance becomes problematic, because all the heavenly scriptures are justice and equity.

The answer is in two respects. The first: it is what we have mentioned repeatedly, that when one thing is expressed by two different attributes, it is permissible to conjoin it with itself, treating the difference between attributes as the difference between essences. Among the examples of this in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided, and who brought forth the pasture﴾ [al-A'la: 1–4]. The referent is one and the attributes are different, and the conjunction is valid because the attributes differ. A parallel from Arab speech is the poet's saying:

"To the lordly king and the son of the hero, and the lion of the battalion in the press."

As for the second respect: it is what the scholar Ibn al-Qayyim—may Allah have mercy on him—pointed to in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in, regarding the general difference between the Book and the Balance.

The explanation: the Book refers to justice and equity as stated explicitly in the heavenly scriptures.

As for the Balance: it includes justice and equity which are not stated explicitly in the heavenly scriptures, but are known from what they have stated explicitly.

So "uff" in His saying: ﴿So do not say to them, "uff"﴾ [al-Isra': 23] is from the Book, because it is explicitly stated in the Book; and forbidding the striking of parents, for example, which is indicated by the prohibition of saying "uff," is from the Balance, that is, from the justice and equity which Allah sent down with His messengers.

And the acceptance of the testimony of two just men in revocation and divorce, stated in His saying: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], is from the Book which Allah sent down, because it is explicitly stated in it.

(p-67) And the acceptance of the testimony of four just men in that is from the Balance which Allah sent down with His messengers.

And the prohibition of consuming the property of orphans, mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa': 10], the verse, is from the Book.

And the prohibition of drowning the property of an orphan and burning it, which is well known from that, is from the Balance which Allah sent down with His messengers.

And the lashing of a male slanderer of a chaste female with eighty lashes, and the rejection of his testimony, and the ruling of his wickedness, stated in His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and do not produce four witnesses—lash them eighty lashes﴾, up to His saying ﴿except those who repent﴾, the verse [al-Nur: 4–5], is from the Book which Allah sent down.

And the punishment of a male slanderer of a male like him, and a female slanderer of a male or a female, with the like of that punishment stated in the Qur'an, is from the aforementioned Balance.

And the lawfulness of a woman who had been irrevocably divorced, by reason of marriage to a second husband and his divorcing her after intercourse, stated in His saying: ﴿And if he divorces her, there is no blame upon them both to return to each other﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], meaning: if the second husband divorces her after intercourse and tasting of the "little honey"—there is no blame upon them both, that is, no blame upon the woman who had been irrevocably divorced, and the husband for whom she had been forbidden, to return to each other after her marriage to the second and his divorce of her—is from the Book which Allah sent down.

As for if the second husband dies after having entered upon her and his death occurred before he divorced her, her lawfulness to the first, for whom she had been forbidden, is from the Balance which Allah sent down with His messengers.

We have pointed to the words of Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned, and given many examples of this in surah al-Anbiya' in our lengthy discussion on His saying: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field﴾, the verse [al-Anbiya': 78].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾

We have already presented the verses clarifying this at the beginning of surah al-Nahl, in the discussion on His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾, the verse [al-Nahl: 1]. And in surah al-Ahzab, in the discussion on His saying: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63]. And in surah al-Mu'min, in the discussion on His saying: ﴿And warn them of the Day of the Approaching﴾, the verse [Ghafir: 18].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 42, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe are apprehensive of it and know that it is the truth.﴾

In this noble verse, He mentions three matters. The first: the disbelievers, who do not believe in the Hour, seek to hasten it, i.e., they ask that it be brought upon them quickly, because of the intensity of their denial of it.

The second: the believers are apprehensive of it, i.e., they fear it.

The third: they know that it is the truth, i.e., that its establishment and its occurrence are true, without any doubt.

All three matters mentioned in this noble verse have been clarified in other places.

As for their seeking to hasten it, we have already presented the verses that clarify it in surah "al-Ra'd" (Thunder), in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good, though exemplary punishments have already passed before them.﴾ [al-Ra'd: 6]. And in other places besides that.

As for the second matter, which is the apprehension and fear of the believers regarding the Hour, He mentioned it in other places, such as:

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who fear their Lord unseen, and who are apprehensive of the Hour.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 49]

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be overturned.﴾ [al-Nur: 37]

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They fulfill vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread.﴾ [al-Insan: 7]

As for the third matter, which is their knowledge that the Hour is true, it is indicated by the verses that explicitly state that there is no doubt about it, since they include the negation of doubt about it for the believers.

The rayb (doubt) is doubt, as in His saying, may He be exalted, concerning those firmly rooted in knowledge: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9], and the verse continues.

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah – there is no deity except Him. He will surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Nisa': 87], and the verse continues.

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾ [Al 'Imran: 25], and the verse continues.

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That you may warn of the Day of Gathering, about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Shura: 7], and the verse continues.

• And His saying, may He be exalted: (p-69) ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and it is He who gives life to the dead, and it is He who is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿And that the Hour is coming, about which there is no doubt, and that Allah will resurrect those in the graves.﴾ [al-Hajj: 6–7]

And other verses besides these.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Unquestionably, those who dispute about the Hour are in extreme error.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify it in surah "al-Furqan" in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Rather, they have denied the Hour, and We have prepared for those who deny the Hour a blaze.﴾ [al-Furqan: 11].

As for His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: yumaruna (dispute), it is the present tense of mara, yumari, mira'an and muma'atan, meaning to argue and contend.

From it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument.﴾ [al-Kahf: 22].

And His saying: ﴿in extreme error﴾, i.e., far from the truth and correctness.

We have already presented the meanings of ḍalal (error) in the Qur'an and the Arabic language, with the evidences, in surah "al-Shu'ara'" in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "I did it then, and I was of the astray."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 20]. And in other places in this blessed book.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 42, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I ask you no reward for it, except kindness to my relatives.﴾ We have already explained in Surat Hud, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And O my people, I ask you for no wealth in return for it﴾ [Hud: 29] - that all the Messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, took no reward for conveying (the message), and we mentioned the verses that indicate this.

In our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book) we mentioned the way of reconciling those verses with this verse of al-Shura, and we said there:

Know first that in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: what al-Sha'bi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah, Abu Malik, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and others, as Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from them: that the meaning of the verse ﴿Say: I ask you no reward for it, except kindness to my relatives﴾ is: except that you show affection to me on account of my kinship which is between me and you, so that you withhold your harm from me and protect me from the harm of people, just as you protect everyone who has a kinship with you like my kinship with you. He (ﷺ) had a relative in every clan of Quraysh. So what he asked of them is not a reward for conveying, because it is offered to everyone, since everyone's relatives show affection to them and defend them against the harm of people.

Abu Talib did this for him, and he did not ask a reward for conveying, because he did not believe.

If he asked no reward except this, which is not a reward, it is established that he asked no reward at all, like the saying of al-Nabigha:

﻿"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched by the clashing of battalions."

This is what the rhetoricians call "affirming praise by means of what resembles blame."

This opinion is the correct one regarding the verse, and Ibn Jarir chose it, and upon it there is no difficulty.

The second: the meaning of the verse ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾ is: do not harm my relatives and my family, and protect me concerning them. This opinion is also narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and upon it too there is no difficulty.

Because affection among Muslims is obligatory among them, and all the more so the kinship of the Prophet (ﷺ). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71]. And in the hadith: "The likeness of the believers in their mercy, their love and their compassion is like one body; when one of its limbs is afflicted, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever." And he (ﷺ) said: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." The hadiths on this are very numerous.

If religion itself requires this among Muslims, it becomes clear that it is not a compensation for conveying.

Some scholars said: the exception is disconnected (munqati') according to both opinions, and upon this too there is no difficulty.

So its meaning according to the first opinion is: "I ask you no reward for it, but I remind you of my kinship among you."

And according to the second: "But I remind you of God concerning my kinship, so protect me concerning them."

The third opinion, and it was said by al-Hasan: ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾ means: except that you seek affection toward God and draw near to Him through obedience and righteous deeds. Upon this too there is no difficulty, because drawing near to God is not a reward for conveying.

(p-71) The fourth opinion: ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾ means: except that you show affection to your relatives and maintain your ties of kinship. Ibn Jarir mentioned this opinion from 'Abd Allah ibn Qasim, and upon it too there is no difficulty.

Because a person's maintaining the ties of his kin is not a reward for conveying.

You have come to know the correct interpretation of the verse, and the resolution of the difficulty has become clear to you regarding all the opinions.

As for the claim that His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾ has been abrogated by His saying: ﴿Say: whatever reward I have asked of you, it is yours﴾ [Saba: 47] - it is weak. And knowledge is with God, may He be exalted. End of quotation.

From what we have mentioned, you have come to know that the first opinion is the correct meaning of the verse.

Yet many people think that the second opinion is the meaning of the verse, so they suppose that the meaning of ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾ is: except that you show affection to me by means of my family members.

Among those who thought this was Muhammad al-Sajjad, when he said to his killer on the day of the Camel: "I remind you of Ha Mim," meaning this Surat al-Shura, and he intended that he is of the family of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so it is incumbent to protect him concerning them, since God, may He be exalted, said in this "Ha Mim": ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾. He meant the stated meaning, thinking it to be what the verse intends. Therefore his killer said concerning that:

"He reminds me of Ha Mim while the spear is shaking, so why did he not recite Ha Mim before advancing?"

We have mentioned this verse and the verses preceding it at the beginning of Surat Hud, and we mentioned that al-Bukhari cited the verse in Surat al-Mu'min, and we mentioned the disagreement about the composer of the verses who killed Muhammad al-Sajjad ibn Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah on the day of the Camel: is he Shurayh ibn Abi Awfa al-'Absi, as al-Bukhari said, or al-Ashtar al-Nakha'i, or 'Isam ibn Muqshi'irr, or Mudlij ibn Ka'b al-Sa'di, or Ka'b ibn Mudlij.

Among those who thought that the meaning of the verse is what Muhammad al-Sajjad thought is al-Kumayt in his saying concerning the family of the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

"We found for you in the family of Ha Mim a verse, which a pious man and an eloquent one among us interpreted."

The verification, if God wills, is that the meaning of the verse is the first opinion: ﴿except kindness to my relatives﴾ (p-72) meaning: except that you show affection to me concerning my kinship among you and protect me concerning it, so that you withhold your harm from me and protect me from the harm of people, as is the way of those who have kinship.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever earns a good deed, We will increase for him therein in goodness.﴾ Al-iqtiraf means al-iktisab (earning, acquiring), i.e., whoever does a good deed of the good deeds and acquires it, We will increase for him therein goodness, i.e., We will multiply it for him.

So the multiplying of good deeds is the increase in their goodness, and this meaning is clarified by verses from the Book of God, may He be exalted:

• Such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa': 40].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who is it that would lend to God a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah and lend God a goodly loan. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves - you will find it with God, better and greater in reward﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20].

So His being "better and greater in reward" is an increase in its goodness, as is not hidden. And so on through other verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 42, verse 25:

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, the Exalted, made clear that He alone is the One who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds. This has been explained in other places, such as:

• The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charity, and that Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful?﴾ [At-Tawbah: 104].

• The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance; perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [At-Tahrim: 8], and the verse continues.

• The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 135].

And other verses besides these.

We have already discussed the meaning of repentance (tawbah), its pillars, and the removal of the difficulties in its pillars, in Surah An-Nur, in our commentary on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And turn to Allah in repentance, all of you, O believers, that you may succeed﴾ [An-Nur: 31].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 42, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But He sends down in due measure whatever He wills﴾.

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that He sends down, in measure (bi-qadar), whatever He wills to send down of provisions and other things; that is, in a known quantity with Him, majestic and exalted. He, majestic and exalted, knows best the wisdom and the benefit in the quantity of everything He sends down. He has clarified this in other places, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]. And other verses besides these.

Allah's saying: ﴿And you cannot escape (Allah) on earth﴾, and so on.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah "al-Nur," in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape (Allah) on earth; their refuge is the Fire﴾ [al-Nur: 57], and so on.

**Allah's saying, the Exalted:** ﴿And among His signs are the ships running upon the sea like mountains.﴾

**His saying, ﴿And among His signs﴾**, means: among His signs, which indicate His power and that He alone deserves to be worshipped, are **al-jawari** (the ships), the singular of which is **jariyah** (ship). From the same root is Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship.﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11], meaning Noah's ark. It was called **jariyah** because it runs (tajri) on the sea.

**His saying, "like mountains,"** means like mountains, and He likened the ships to mountains because of their size.

It is reported from Mujahid that **al-a'lam** (the landmarks) means the palaces. It is reported from al-Khalil that the Arabs call every elevated thing an **'alam** (landmark), and the plural of **'alam** is **a'lam**.

What al-Khalil mentioned is well known in the language, and from the same usage is the saying of al-Khansa', lamenting her brother Sakhr:

*Indeed Sakhr is one whom the guided ones take as a model,*
*as if he were a landmark with a fire on its top.*

What this noble verse contains, that the sailing of ships on the sea is among His signs indicating His perfect power, has been explained in other places, such as:

• Allah's saying: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship. And We have created for them of its likeness that which they ride. And if We willed, We would drown them, and there would be no one to shout for them, nor would they be saved, except as a mercy from Us and enjoyment for a time.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41–44].

• And His saying: ﴿And We left it as a sign for the worlds.﴾ [al-Ankabut: 15] (referring to the ark) — more precisely: ﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship and made it a sign for the worlds.﴾ [al-Ankabut: 15].

• And His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ships which run in the sea with that which benefits people…﴾, up to His saying: ﴿are signs for a people who reason.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164].

• And His saying in Surat "al-Nahl": ﴿And you see the ships plowing through it, that you may seek of His bounty…﴾ [the verse; cited here as Maryam: 14].

• And His saying in "Fatir": (p-74) ﴿And you see the ships therein plowing through, that you may seek of His bounty…﴾ [the verse; Fatir: 12].

Verses of this kind are many and well known.

**As for the readings (qira'at)** of this word: Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read **al-jawari** with a silent **ya'** after the **ra'** when continuing (wasl) only, not when pausing (waqf). Ibn Kathir read it with the **ya'** mentioned both in continuation and in pause. The rest read **al-jiwar** with the **ya'** omitted both in continuation and in pause.

The Exalted said: ﴿And those who avoid the major sins and the abominations﴾.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this word as كَبِيرَ الإثْمِ (*kabira al-ithm*), with a kasra on the ba', a sakin ya' after it, and a ra', in the singular form.

The rest of the readers read it as كَبائِرَ الإثْمِ (*kaba'ira al-ithm*), with a fatha on the ba', an alif after it, then a hamza with a kasra before the ra', in the plural form.

His saying "those who" (*wal-ladhina*) is in the genitive position as a conjunction (*'atf*) on His saying: ﴿And what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord﴾. The meaning is: "And better and more lasting also for those who avoid the major sins and the abominations."

*Al-fawahish* is the plural of *fahisha*. The verified view, God willing, is that the abominations are among the major sins.

The more apparent view is that they are among the worst of them, because *al-fahisha* in the language is a trait that has reached the extreme of ugliness, and everyone who is excessive in something and goes to extremes in it is *fahish* in it.

From this is the saying of Tarafa ibn al-'Abd in his Mu'allaqa:

*I see death selecting the noble and choosing
the choicest wealth of the stingy, excessive one.*

So his saying *al-fahish* means the one who goes to extremes in stinginess, to the utmost degree.

What this noble verse contains of the true promise of the Exalted to those who avoid the major sins and the abominations, of the reward that is with Him for them, which is better and more lasting, has come explained in another place. The Exalted explained in Surat al-Nisa' that among that is His expiating their evil deeds and admitting them to a noble abode, which is Paradise, in His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds and admit you to a noble entrance﴾ [al-Nisa': 31]. And in Surat al-Najm He explained that by avoiding the major sins and the abominations they truly deserve the name of *al-muhsinun* (the doers of good), and He promised them the best reward (*al-husna*) for that.

(p-75) The more apparent view is that the best reward is Paradise. What supports this is the hadith: "*Al-husna* is Paradise, and the increase is looking at the Noble Face of Allah," in the explanation of His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus: 26], as we have already mentioned.

The verse of Surat al-Najm mentioned is His saying: ﴿And that He may reward those who did good with the best reward﴾ [al-Najm: 31]. Then He explained who is meant by "those who did good" in His saying: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the abominations, except for minor lapses. Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ [al-Najm: 32].

The most apparent of the opinions on His saying "except for minor lapses" (*illa al-lamam*) is that *al-lamam* means minor sins. Among the clearest Qur'anic verses on this is His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 31]. It indicates that avoiding the major sins is a cause for the forgiveness of minor sins, and the best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

What supports this is the authentic hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in the Sahih, who said: "I have not seen anything more like *al-lamam* than what Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Allah has written for the son of Adam his portion of adultery; he will inevitably encounter it. The adultery of the eye is the look, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul wishes and desires, and the private part either confirms that or denies it.'"

On this view, the exception in His saying "except for minor lapses" is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), because *al-lamam*, which is the minor sins according to this view, does not fall within the major sins and the abominations. We have already set out the verification of this matter regarding the disjunctive exception in Surat Maryam, in discussing His saying: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, only the word "Peace"﴾ [Maryam: 62].

A group of the people of knowledge said: the exception is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*). They said: according to this, the meaning of ﴿except for minor lapses﴾ is: except that one commits an abomination once, then avoids it and does not return to it afterwards.

They used as evidence for this the words of the rajaz poet:

*If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much,
and what servant of Yours is there who has not sinned?*

Ibn Jarir, al-Tirmidhi and others related this verse as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report. Its soundness as a marfu' report is questionable.

(p-76) Some scholars said: *al-lamam* means what they committed before entering Islam of disbelief and sins. Its remoteness is not hidden.

The most apparent of the opinions is what we have mentioned, because of the indication of the aforementioned verse of Surat al-Nisa' for it, and the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, which is agreed upon (in the two Sahihs).

Know that the major sins are not limited to a specific number. Some of them have been specified, such as "the seven destructive sins" (*al-sab' al-muwbiqat*), meaning those that destroy because of their magnitude. It has been established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that they are: "Associating partners with Allah, killing a soul that Allah has forbidden except by right, sorcery, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, fleeing on the day of battle, and slandering chaste, unwary, believing women."

Many reports have come from the Prophet (ﷺ) specifying some of the major sins, such as disobedience to parents, violating the sanctity of the Sacred House of Allah, returning to the desert after the migration, drinking wine, the perjurious oath (*al-yamin al-ghamus*), theft, withholding surplus water, withholding surplus pasture, and false testimony.

In some reports established in the Sahih from Ibn Mas'ud, "the greatest of the major sins is associating partners with Allah, who created the creation; then a man killing his child for fear that he would eat with him; then committing adultery with his neighbour's wife." In some of them also: "that among the major sins is a man causing his parents to be cursed." In some of them also: "that abusing a Muslim is wickedness (*fusuq*) and fighting him is disbelief (*kufr*)." That indicates that these two are among the major sins.

In some reports: "that among the major sins is slandering a Muslim's honour, and reviling a man with the reproach (*al-sabbatayn bil-sabba*)."

In some reports: "that among them is combining the two prayers without an excuse."

In some of them: "that among them is despairing of the mercy of Allah, and feeling secure from the plan of Allah." What indicates these two is His saying: ﴿Indeed, none despair of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf: 87], and His saying: ﴿So none feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾ [al-A'raf: 99].

In some of them: "that among them is evil thinking about Allah." What supports it is His saying: ﴿And He will punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women who think about Allah an evil thought. Upon them is a circle of evil; Allah has become angry with them, cursed them, and prepared for them Hell, and it is an evil destination﴾ [al-Fath: 6].

In some of them: "that among them is harming in a bequest."

(p-77) In some of them: "that among them is embezzlement (*ghulul*)." What supports it is His saying: ﴿And whoever embezzles will bring what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161]. We mentioned the meaning of embezzlement in Surat al-Anfal and mentioned the ruling on the embezzler.

In some of them: "that among the people of the major sins are those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price." What supports it is His saying: ﴿Those will have no share in the Hereafter, Allah will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77].

We have not mentioned the chains of narration (*asanid*) of these reports or the texts of their wording, for fear of lengthening. Some of their chains are not free from scrutiny, but almost none of them is free from some sound supporting evidence from the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ).

Know that the people of knowledge differed on the definition of the major sin. Some of them said: it is every sin that merits a legal penalty (*hadd*) from the limits of Allah.

Some of them said: it is every sin for which a threat has come with fire, a curse, anger, or punishment.

Some later scholars chose as the definition of the major sin that it is every sin that indicates its perpetrator's lack of concern for the religion.

From Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that the major sins are closer to seventy than to seven. And from him also that they are closer to seven hundred than to seven.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The verified view is that they are not confined to seven, and that what the hadiths indicate, that they are seven, does not require their being confined to that number. That is because it only indicates the negation of what is other than the seven by implication (*mafhum*), and this is an implication of the title (*mafhum laqab*), and the correct view is that it is not considered valid.

Even if we say that it is an implication of number (*mafhum 'adad*), it would still not be considered valid, because the addition of major sins beyond the seven is indicated explicitly (*mantuq*).

Indeed, a number more than seven has come in the Sahih, and the explicit statement takes precedence over the implication, although the implication of number is not among the strongest implications.

The more apparent view to me as a criterion of the major sin is that it is every sin accompanied by something indicating that it is greater than mere disobedience, whether that is a threat of fire, anger, a curse or punishment, or whether a legal penalty is required for it, or other things that indicate the intensification and emphasis of its prohibition.

(p-78) Although some people of knowledge said: every sin is a major sin. And His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 31], and His saying: ﴿except for minor lapses﴾ [al-Najm: 32], indicate that they are not equal, and that some acts of disobedience are major sins and some are minor sins. And what is well known among the people of knowledge is that there is no minor sin with persistence (*al-israr*), and no major sin with seeking forgiveness (*al-istighfar*). And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 42, verse 40:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in the end of Surah "An-Nahl" in the discussion of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾ [An-Nahl: 126]. And in Surah "Az-Zumar," in the discussion of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾ [Az-Zumar: 17-18].

Allah's saying: ﴿And whoever defends himself after he has been wronged, those – there is no route of blame against them.﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in our discussion of the verse in "An-Nahl" and the verse in "Az-Zumar," which were mentioned just above.

Allah's statement: ﴿And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment…﴾ [the verse].

We have already presented the verses clarifying this in Surah "al-A'raf," in the discussion of His statement: ﴿So do we have any intercessors who will intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might act differently from what we used to do?﴾ [the verse] [Al-A'raf: 53].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah ash-Shura

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will see them exposed to it, humbled by humiliation, looking with a furtive glance﴾, to the end of the verse.

This noble verse indicates that the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection will look with hidden eyes of weak sight. Another verse has come which gives the impression of something contrary to this, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We have removed from you your veil, and your sight this Day is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22].

The answer is what the author of al-Itqan (al-Suyuti, al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an) mentioned: that what is meant by the sharpness of sight is knowledge and strength of awareness. Qutrub said: "fabasaruka" means your knowledge, and your awareness of it is strong, from their saying "basura bi-kadha," meaning he knew it. What is meant is not the seeing of the eye. Al-Farisi said: what indicates this is His saying: ﴿So We have removed from you your veil﴾.

Some scholars also said: ﴿your sight this Day is sharp﴾ means you perceive by it what you were blind to in the life of this world. What supports this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us﴾ to the end of the verse [As-Sajdah: 12]; and His saying: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are going to fall into it﴾ to the end of the verse [Al-Kahf: 53]; and His saying: ﴿How clearly they will hear and see on the Day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in clear error﴾ [Maryam: 38].

The indication of the Qur'an for this last view is apparent, so it is likely the stronger, although the author of al-Itqan limited himself to the first.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 42, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit (rūḥ) of Our command﴾.

We have already presented the verses clarifying this in the beginning of Surah "al-Naḥl," in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He sends down the angels with the spirit of His command upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Naḥl: 2], and so on.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith (al-īmān) was, but We made it a light by which We guide whomever We will of Our servants﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿You did not know what the Book was nor what faith was﴾ — Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explains in it His favour upon this noble Prophet, that He taught him this great Qur'an, which he did not know before that, and taught him the details of the religion of Islam, which he did not know before that.

So His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was﴾ means: you did not know what this Book is, which is the Great Qur'an, until I taught it to you. And "You did not know what faith was," which is the details of this Islamic religion, until I taught you.

It is well known that the truth without doubt, which is the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamā'ah), is that faith (īmān) encompasses speech and action along with belief (i'tiqād).

This is established in many authentic hadiths, among them the well-known hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, and among them the hadith: "Whoever stands in prayer during Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward..." — the hadith continues — where he named the standing in prayer during Ramadan as faith. And the hadith: "Faith has seventy-odd branches (bid' wa-sab'ūn shu'bah)," and in some of its narrations "sixty-odd branches, the highest of which is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the lowest of which is removing harm from the road."

The hadiths of this kind are numerous, and what al-Bayhaqī reported in Shu'ab al-Īmān suffices in this regard. He, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, did not know the details of the obligatory prayers and their times, nor the fast of Ramadan and what is permissible in it and what is not, and he did not know the details of zakat, nor what property it is obligatory upon, nor the threshold (niṣāb) and the amount due from it, nor the details of the pilgrimage (ḥajj), and the like. This is what is meant by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿nor faith﴾.

What He mentions here, that he did not know these matters until He taught him them by revealing to him this great light, which is the Book of Allah, has come in other places, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom, and taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisā': 113], and His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories by revealing to you this Qur'an, though before it you were certainly among the unaware﴾ [Yūsuf: 3].

His saying in this verse of Yusuf: ﴿though before it you were certainly among the unaware﴾ is like His saying here: ﴿You did not know what the Book was nor what faith was﴾, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 7], according to the most correct interpretations, as we have presented in Surah "al-Shu'arā'" in the discussion of His saying: ﴿He said: I did it then, while I was among the astray﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 20], and other verses besides these.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿But We made it a light by which We guide whomever We will﴾, the pronoun in His saying "We made it" (ja'alnāhu) refers to the Great Qur'an mentioned in His saying: ﴿a spirit of Our command﴾. (p-80) And His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was﴾ means: but We made this Great Qur'an a light by which We guide whomever We will of Our servants to its guidance.

The Qur'an is called "light" because it illuminates the truth and removes the darknesses of ignorance, doubt and polytheism.

What he mentions here, that this Qur'an is a light, has come clarified in other verses, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [al-Nisā': 174].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and follow the light that was sent down with him﴾ [al-A'rāf: 157].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book, by which Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace and brings them out of darknesses into light by His permission and guides them to a straight path﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 15-16].

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger and the light which We have sent down﴾ [al-Taghābun: 8].

What these noble verses indicate, that this Qur'an is a light, shows that it is what uncovers the darknesses of ignorance, in whose light the truth appears, is distinguished from falsehood, and by which good is distinguished from evil and guidance from error, and the good from the ugly.

It is therefore obligatory upon every Muslim to be illuminated by its light: to hold its beliefs, to make lawful what it makes lawful, to forbid what it forbids, to comply with its commands, to avoid what it prohibits, and to take lessons from its stories and parables.

The entire Sunnah is included in acting upon it, due to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 7].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾.

The straight path has been explained by Him, may He be exalted, in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have earned Your anger or of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 6-7].

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And indeed you guide﴾ and so on, we have already presented the verses clarifying it in Surah "Fuṣṣilat" in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ and so on [Fuṣṣilat: 17], and we explained there the way of reconciling His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ with His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 56].

(p-81) The "ṣirāṭ" in the language of the Arabs is the clear road, and "mustaqīm" is that which has no crookedness in it. From this is the saying of Jarīr:

Commander of the Believers, upon a path that stays straight when the watering-places become crooked.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 42, verse 53:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

What this noble verse contains, namely that all matters return to Allah, meaning they go back to Him alone and not to anyone else, has been clarified in other verses, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the whole matter will be returned﴾ [Hud: 123]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [Al 'Imran: 109]. And ﴿You are the best nation produced for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. And other verses besides these.
